name: Afamelanotide
lead: Afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse and originally called melanotan I, is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) that is delivered as a subcutaneous implant. It is approved to reduce phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited condition in which light exposure causes severe pain [1][4].

It is a melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) agonist that increases melanin production and therefore darkens the skin [1][4]. Because of this, it is often mentioned in looksmaxxing forums alongside the unlicensed peptide melanotan II, although the two are different molecules with different regulatory standing; afamelanotide is a prescription drug for a specific disease, while melanotan II has no approval [3][25].

Its best-supported evidence is from randomized, placebo-controlled trials in EPP, in which it increased pain-free time in light [5]. Smaller or exploratory studies have examined it in vitiligo, acne, solar urticaria, Hailey-Hailey disease and other conditions [11][15][16][14]. No trial has tested it as a cosmetic tanning product in healthy people on a large scale, and its approval does not extend to cosmetic use.

paras: In the European Union, afamelanotide is indicated for preventing phototoxicity in adults with EPP; in the United States the label is to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with a history of phototoxic reactions from EPP [1][4]. EPP is a photodermatosis in which accumulated protoporphyrin causes painful reactions to light, and treatments had been limited [6].

Afamelanotide's tanning effect is the reason forum users discuss it. Posters on looksmax.org talk about melanotan 1 as an alternative to melanotan 2 for tanning and note that it can darken freckles [23][25][26]. The approved product is a prescription implant used in specialist centres rather than a consumer tanning product [4].

Erythropoietic protoporphyria: two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials tested 16 mg afamelanotide implants given every 60 days in 74 European and 94 US patients. In the US trial, pain-free time in direct sunlight at six months was longer with afamelanotide; quality of life was also assessed [5]. A 2009 report described earlier clinical responses in EPP patients [6][9]. A long-term observational study followed 115 patients [7], and an immunogenicity evaluation measured antibodies in EPP patients across phase 2 and 3 trials [8]. The label's safety data come from three vehicle-controlled trials involving 244 adults [4].

Vitiligo: a randomized multicenter trial compared afamelanotide implant plus narrowband UVB (n=28) with UVB alone (n=27) in adults with non-segmental vitiligo [11]. An earlier report described four patients [12], and a randomized study examined the combination in Asian patients [13]. Reviews describe afamelanotide among emerging vitiligo options and note that no fully satisfactory vitiligo treatment exists [17].

Other conditions: phase 2 studies examined it in acne vulgaris [15][21], Hailey-Hailey disease [14] and solar urticaria [16]. Small registered studies cover xeroderma pigmentosum, DNA repair after UV in healthy volunteers, and acute ischaemic stroke [18][19][20]. An exploratory 2026 study assessed its effect on UV erythema and melanogenic responses in healthy humans [22].
These other-condition studies are small and exploratory, and none has produced a cosmetic indication.

In trials, the most commonly reported effects were implant-site reactions (21 percent), headache (20 percent) and nausea (19 percent) [1]. Less common effects include back pain, fatigue, dizziness, flushing, new moles and freckles, and rarely hypersensitivity reactions [1].

The US label warns of serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, in post-marketing use, and of generalized skin darkening and darkening of existing naevi and freckles; it recommends regular skin monitoring [4]. Full body skin examinations every six months are often recommended [1].

Afamelanotide is a synthetic tridecapeptide analogue of alpha-MSH that binds predominantly to MC1R. It resists breakdown by proteolytic enzymes and binds longer than natural alpha-MSH, producing darkening of the skin through increased eumelanin [1][2]. In EPP, the increase in pigmentation is associated with greater tolerance of light [5].

Afamelanotide was among the alpha-MSH analogues synthesised at the University of Arizona in the 1980s as potential sunless tanning agents, under the name melanotan I. A technology-transfer company licensed it to Australian start-up Epitan, which became Clinuvel in 2006. The FDA approved it in 2019 [3].

On looksmax.org, guides describe melanotan 1 and 2 together as alpha-MSH tanning peptides and some posts note that melanotan 1 can cause spontaneous arousal [24]. Forum users compare the two, describing melanotan 1 as having a more extensively researched safety profile and producing slower tanning than melanotan 2 [25][26]. Peptide products sold outside of prescription channels are not the licensed Scenesse implant [3].
Registered studies continue in xeroderma pigmentosum, facial vitiligo and DNA repair, mostly small phase 1-2 designs [17][18].

lore.intro: Forum users on looksmax.org discuss afamelanotide as 'melanotan 1', usually in comparison with melanotan 2 [24][25][26].

claims.believers: Forum posters say MT1 has a better safety profile because it is more extensively researched and hits fewer receptors [25].
claims.experts: Afamelanotide has controlled trials in EPP and an FDA label with hypersensitivity and naevus-darkening warnings; melanotan II has no approval [4][5][3]. Gray-market products are not the licensed implant.

claims.claim: MT1 causes fewer moles than MT2
claims.believers: Users say moles are 'far less proven' with MT1 but note it tans slower; some argue the difference reflects potency rather than risk [26].
claims.experts: The label warns that afamelanotide darkens pre-existing naevi and recommends skin checks [4]. A melanoma case has been reported in a melanotan user [27].

claims.believers: A forum reply confirms that it makes freckles darker and describes them as attractive [23].
claims.experts: The label and trial reports list darkening of pre-existing freckles as an expected effect [4][1].

claims.claim: Melanotan can reduce UV damage over time
claims.believers: A forum compendium states that melanotan induces pigmentation and can reduce UV damage to skin over time [24].
claims.experts: In EPP, afamelanotide raised tolerance of light [5]. A 2026 exploratory study examined its UV responses in healthy people [22]. Its use as a general photoprotectant is not an approved indication [4].

claims.believers: A reply notes that melanotan 1 can produce spontaneous sexual arousal in men and women [24].
claims.experts: Erectile effects are documented in controlled studies of melanotan II, a different compound [3]. No trial reviewed for this article reports it as an outcome for afamelanotide.
